Some houses are built for arrival. Garran Hill was built for return.

The Estate

A 1916 Neo-Georgian estate, restored to the studs.

Built for Walter Hines Page, United States Ambassador to the Court of St James's, and held by a line of stewards for more than a century. Rare handmade red brick laid in Flemish bond above a classic water table. The same craftsmen who built Pinehurst built this house. Restored 1999 to 2001: plumbing, electrical, and climate systems replaced, custom Marvin windows throughout, Georgian millwork integrated room by room.

The Living Room

Seven mantels survive. This is the first.

Carved in 1916 and never painted over. French doors open the room to the rear terrace, the way the house has received its guests for a century.

The Library

Floor to ceiling, wall to wall.

Shelving for a working library, a fireplace for reading past midnight. The room a publisher's house was always going to have.

The Sitting Room

Delft tile, and a staircase that surprises.

Hand painted Dutch tile surrounds the fire. A spiral staircase turns up from the corner, original to the house and still in daily use.

The Kitchen

Heart pine, black granite, morning light.

Reclaimed heart pine cabinetry under a wall of windows. A butler's pantry with the original farm sink connects to the dining room, as it did in 1916.

The Primary Wing

A first floor suite, a wing of its own.

The primary occupies its own wing on the main level. Morning sun, garden views, and a marble bath fitted during the restoration.

The Grounds

Four acres, walled and planted.

A saltwater pool inside a brick walled garden. Two lighted regulation tennis courts ready for new surfaces. A camellia garden, mature longleaf pines, and the Wee Cottage playhouse at the edge of the lawn.

Provenance

A century of stewardship, documented.

Walter Hines Page. Betty Dumaine and the Princess Mother of Thailand. The 1999 restoration recorded in fifteen architectural drawings. Every claim cited.

Read the full history →
The Last Parcel

The original estate ran to a thousand acres. Over the decades it was divided, and a neighborhood grew around the house and took its name.

What remains is this: the house, its gardens, its pool and courts, on the last piece of the original Garran Hill still on its own ground.

The house was not built for spectacle. It was built for coming back.
